Michael Bauer Smith Sr.

Grace's father-in-law · a family from the records

Michael Bauer Smith Sr.

Terre Haute, Indiana, 1949 · Santa Clara · San Mateo. The son of a Terre Haute laboratory technician who became a Sunnyvale rocket-plant technician, and of an upholsterer's daughter from Poplar Street; the grandson of a First World War private and a Lower Austrian immigrant; a Vietnam veteran, airborne; the husband of Betty Goodwin and the father of Michael, Jason, Robert, Dawn and Michelle. Four generations of his people lived in Terre Haute, and this page follows them back to Kentucky, Ohio and a village on the Danube.

Compiled 4 and 5 September 2026 for the Smith and Goodwin families by Grace Marie Goodwin, from the census, the Vigo County records, the Army's files, the Terre Haute Tribune and the cemeteries of Terre Haute and Santa Clara. A companion to Goodwin & Oviatt Lines and to the page for Robert Charles Goodwin, Betty's father.

Twelve chapters

The family, in order

Everything below rests on a record named in the sources at the end; where the records fall silent, or where the family's own knowledge is the only source, the text says so. Michael is living, and his own chapter keeps to what his family has said.

Terre Haute, Indiana, 1949

Two rooms on South Fifteenth Street

Michael Bauer Smith was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1949, the first child of Ralph Warren Smith and Patricia Antoinette Bauer, who had been married a year. His middle name is his mother's maiden name, and it carries the whole of one side of this page: the Bauers of Poplar Street, an upholsterer from Lower Austria and the Terre Haute girl he married in 1908. His first name was new to both families.

The census taker who came to 43 South 15th Street on the first of April 1950 found the three of them together and wrote the baby down as 'Michael B, son, 0.' Ralph, 23, was a laboratory technician working a 46-hour week, and Patricia, 22, kept the house. The rooms themselves have a small footnote in the newspaper: on 4 September 1949 the Terre Haute Tribune carried a classified advertisement for '43 S. 15th, 2 unfurnished modern rooms, share bath, prefer couple with child,' and a young couple with a new baby answered a description like that exactly. Whether the Smiths were the couple who took those rooms the records do not say, but seven months later they were living at that address.

The Terre Haute that Michael was born into was a factory and railroad town of 65,000 on the Wabash, with the Commercial Solvents plant, where his father had been a watchman in 1948, turning out industrial alcohol and, since the war, penicillin; it was the town where every one of his grandparents and great-grandparents on both sides had lived for the best part of a century, and where his great-grandfather Anton Bauer still ran an upholstery shop on Poplar Street at 66, sixty hours a week. While Michael was still a boy the family went west, and the rest of his own story belongs to California and to the people who can tell it: Santa Clara as a boy, the Army and a paratrooper's wings in the Vietnam years, and more than thirty years in San Mateo with Betty and their five children. This page is about where he came from.

Honey Creek Township, 1926 to 1944

Ralph Warren Smith, a farm boy on Spring Hill Road

Michael's father, Ralph Warren Smith, was born on 28 May 1926 in Honey Creek Township, the farming country just south of Terre Haute, the fifth and last child of Pearl Ruby Smith and Jessie Ethel Hults. The clerk who filled in Indiana birth certificate number 26489 spelled him 'Ralph Warn Smith'; the family would later turn the names around and call him Warren, which is how the 1940 census taker heard it. His birthday was one of the small facts he adjusted for the Army: on his draft card, his enlistment papers and his veteran's file he was born on 15 May 1926, and on his marriage license at eighteen he was born in 1923, but the birth certificate, his obituary and his headstone all say 28 May.

In April 1930 the census found the family on Spring Hill Road in Honey Creek Township: Pearl, 35, and Jessie, 31, with Jessie Maxine, 11, Richard Eugene, 9, Paul, 7, Donald, 6, and Ralph, 3. They were still there in 1940, farming, and Ralph at 13 had finished the seventh grade. By the time he registered for the draft on 15 May 1944 the family's address was Terre Haute and he was six feet tall and 165 pounds, with brown hair, blue eyes and a light complexion, and his next of kin was his father Pearl. He had four years of high school by the time the Army took him that autumn.

Indianapolis to Tokyo, 1944 to 1946

Private Smith, 35908327, 1st Cavalry Division

Ralph was inducted into the Army of the United States at Indianapolis on 9 September 1944, three months after his eighteenth birthday, a private, single, with four years of high school, serial number 35908327. The Army's own record of his service is thin, since his personnel file has not been found, but the draft card he filled out in 1948 sets down the frame of it in his own words: active duty from 9 September 1944, the Army, the 1st Cavalry Division, discharged 22 November 1946. Twenty-six months.

The 1st Cavalry Division was in the Philippines when Ralph went into uniform. It had landed on Leyte in October 1944 and on Luzon in January 1945, and its flying column was the first American unit into Manila on 3 February 1945; when Japan surrendered it went ashore at Yokohama and, on 8 September 1945, became the first division to enter Tokyo, where it stayed as an occupation force for five years. A soldier who enlisted in September 1944 would have finished his training early in 1945 and shipped out as a replacement, joining the division either in the last fighting on Luzon that spring or in Japan that autumn; the discharge fourteen months after the war ended points to the occupation, a nineteen-year-old from Honey Creek Township walking the streets of Tokyo. Which of those it was, his own discharge papers would say, and they are among the things this page still has to find.

He came home once in the middle of it. On 26 January 1945, four and a half months after his induction, Ralph W. Smith, 'age 22, born 15 May 1923,' married Florence Jane Francis, a Prairieton Township girl a few months younger than himself, in Vigo County. He was eighteen; the extra years were for the license. It was a wartime furlough wedding, and it did not survive the war. By 1948 they were divorced, and in April 1949 Florence married Richard Norman Fields. The story has a coda sixty years on.

Terre Haute, 1948

A watchman at Commercial Solvents marries a secretary from Poplar Street

Ralph came back to Terre Haute and to work at the Commercial Solvents Corporation, the chemical plant on the north side of town that had grown from a wartime distillery into the largest penicillin plant in the world. On 13 June 1948 the Terre Haute Tribune's list of marriages included 'Ralph W. Smith, Terre Haute, Commercial Solvents employee, and Patricia A. Bauer, Terre Haute, secretary.' They had been married on 28 May 1948, his twenty-second birthday, at Terre Haute, by Samuel C. McQueen; the license gives her parents as Anton Bauer and Belle Bean, the clerk's spelling of Beam, and his as Pearl R. Smith and Jessie E. Hults. She was twenty, born on 1 March 1928, the tenth of the eleven Bauer children.

When Ralph registered again under the new draft law on 8 September 1948 he was married, a watchman at 'Commercial Solvonts,' six feet and 170 pounds, brown hair, blue eyes, fair, and his next of kin was his mother Jessie. By the census of 1950 he had moved up to laboratory technician. Michael was born between the two.

Frauendorf to Poplar Street, 1883 to 1908

Anton Bauer, the upholsterer from Lower Austria

Michael's great-grandfather Anton Bauer was born on 7 May 1883 at Frauendorf, a farming village of a few hundred people in the Tullnerfeld, the flat, fertile plain along the Danube east of Traismauer in Lower Austria, an hour from Vienna. His parents were Florian Bauer, born in 1844, and Barbara Crites, as the Terre Haute registrar spelled her name on his death certificate ninety-four years later, born in 1850; the cousins' trees on Ancestry give the parents' deaths at Frauendorf in 1927 and 1935, so they stayed. The village belonged to the parish of Stollhofen, whose baptismal register for 1881 to 1907 is online at the Diocese of St. Poelten's Matricula archive and should hold his christening, in the priest's Latin, with his godparents and the house number; that is one of the pages still to be read. His brothers and sisters scattered the way Austrian villagers did in those years: Josephine, born 1876, and Florian, born 1890, both died in Tuscarawas County, Ohio, and Theresia, born 1879, died at Frauendorf in 1973.

Anton left for America in 1901, at eighteen, and by the spring of 1908 he was in Terre Haute; on 14 May 1908 he married Ida Belle Beam there, a wagon maker's daughter of eighteen, and the 1910 census found them at 309 Poplar Street with a year-old daughter, Anna Belle, Anton an upholsterer for a dry goods store, renting, 26, 'born Germany' to the enumerator's ear, which in Terre Haute was how an Austrian's accent sounded. He registered for the draft in 1917 at 1100 Poplar Street, short, medium build, blue eyes and 'slightly bald' at 34, and 1100 Poplar was the family's address for the next forty years. The censuses watch the shop grow: a finisher in a furniture factory in 1920; by 1930 an upholsterer 'working on own account' in a shop of his own, owning the house, valued at $5,000; in 1940 the proprietor of an upholstery business, eight years of schooling, fifty hours a week; and in 1950, at 66, still 'repairing and upholstering' in his own shop, sixty hours a week, with Ida Belle, their son Joseph, 20, their daughter Helen McGee and her two-year-old Mary under the same roof.

The Terre Haute Tribune carried his shop's line in the classifieds through the 1950s, 'Upholstering, repairs, Anton Bauer,' and on 10 May 1971 its 'Nosey News Hawk' column noted that 'Anton Bauer, 2800 Kussner Ave., celebrated his 88th birthday last Friday. A life-long resident of Terre Haute, he was owner and operator of the Anton Bauer Upholstery Co. for years. Now retired, he keeps busy in his large garden.' He died in Terre Haute on 2 March 1977, at 93, and was buried with Ida Belle in Calvary Cemetery, the Catholic cemetery, under a stone that gives their years and a cross. His citizenship is a small puzzle: the 1920 census called him naturalized, the 1930 census an alien, the 1940 census a man with first papers, and the 1950 census a citizen. An Anton Bauer 'born 1883 in Austria, arrived 1900' was naturalized at Milwaukee on 14 June 1906, and one family tree has attached that record to him, but another Anton Bauer of the same age, born in Bohemia, was living in Milwaukee in 1910 and died there in 1968, and the Milwaukee paper is more likely his.

Poplar Street, 1909 to 1973

Ida Belle Beam and the house of eleven children

Ida Belle Beam, Michael's great-grandmother, was born on 6 August 1889 in Indiana, the eldest child of Jacob Beam, a wagon maker born in Indiana in November 1851, and Emma Alice Winters, whom he had married in Vigo County on 12 November 1888. The 1900 census found the Beams renting at 1910 Eighteenth Street in Terre Haute, Jacob 48 at his trade, with Lillian, 10, which was Ida Belle's first name on paper, Ruby, 7, and James, 3. Her cousins on Ancestry know her as Lillian Ida Belle; her husband's draft cards, the census and her own death certificate call her Ida Belle, and so did the Tribune.

Between 1909 and 1929 she had eleven children at 1100 Poplar Street: Anna Belle in January 1909, Margaret in 1911, a son Anton who lived from August 1912 to June 1913, Frances Josephine in 1914, Rose Marie in 1916, Mary Elizabeth in 1919, Anton Joseph junior in 1920, Helen Angela in 1923, Betty about 1925, Patricia Antoinette on 1 March 1928, and Joseph Anton in May 1929. Ten of them were alive when the census taker counted the house in 1930, from Annabelle, 21, to Joseph, 0, and six of them, Mary, Anton junior, Helen, Betty, Patricia and Joseph, were still at home with their parents in 1940. The family were parishioners of St. Patrick's, the Catholic church a few blocks from the house.

Ida Belle died at 10 o'clock on the night of Sunday, 25 March 1973, at 83, at home at 2800 Kussner Street, where she and Anton had moved after the shop closed. The Tribune's notice the next day listed 'the husband, Anton Sr.; two sons, Anton Jr. and Joseph, both of Terre Haute; eight daughters, Mrs. Rose Gantz, Mrs. Margaret Hoffman and Mrs. Helen McGee, all of Terre Haute, Mrs. Annabelle Sullivan,' and the rest, where the microfilm copy of the column breaks off; the eight daughters living were Annabelle, Margaret, Frances, Rose, Mary, Helen, Betty and Patricia, the last of them by then a Santa Clara, California, housewife of 45. The Mass of the Resurrection was said for her at St. Patrick's on the Wednesday, and she was buried at Calvary. Anton followed her four years later, almost to the month.

Honey Creek Township and the Ohio River, 1894 to 1919

Pearl Ruby Smith: a farm boy's name, a private's war and a wedding at the river

Michael's grandfather Pearl Ruby Smith was born on 8 November 1894 in Vigo County, the second child of Garrett R. Smith and Sarah Elizabeth Killen, and he carried a name that the census takers never got used to: the enumerator of 1900, finding a five-year-old Pearl in Garrett's house in Honey Creek Township, wrote 'daughter.' He grew up on rented farms south of Terre Haute, at Honey Creek in 1900 and Riley in 1910, one of six children.

On 5 June 1917 he registered for the draft at Terre Haute, single, a farmer on a rural mail route, with light brown hair and light brown eyes, and on 21 September 1917 the Army took him: Private Pearl R. Smith, serial number 1,986,564. The Indiana men called up that September went, for the most part, to Camp Zachary Taylor at Louisville, Kentucky, the new cantonment where the 84th Division was being built, and the date and place of his wedding fit that camp. On 24 November 1917, nine weeks after he went into the Army, Pearl married Jessie Ethel Hults, 19, in Clark County, Indiana, which is Jeffersonville, across the Ohio River from Louisville and the camp. She had come down from Terre Haute to marry him before he went overseas. He was discharged on 18 April 1919, after nineteen months, long enough for a tour in France with the 84th or with one of the divisions its men were sent to fill, and the government marker on his grave says all that his family asked it to say: Pvt, US Army, World War I.

Their first child, Jessie Maxine, was born on 2 January 1919 while he was still in uniform. Richard Eugene followed in 1921, Paul in 1922, Donald Garrett in 1923 and Ralph Warren in 1926, and the family farmed on Spring Hill Road in Honey Creek Township through the thirties. The marriage broke in the last year of the war, when a Vigo County court divorced them in November 1944, two months after Ralph left for the Army, and it mended: on 8 November 1945 Pearl R. Smith and Jessie E. Smith, 47, of Terre Haute, married each other again. Pearl died in Terre Haute on 15 March 1978, at 83, and Jessie on 1 September 1991, at 93, the widow of Pearl R. Smith, as the Indianapolis Star's list of Indiana deaths put it; they lie together at Roselawn Memorial Park.

Lost Creek Township, 1841 to 1957

Jessie Ethel Hults: the Hults farm and the Eversoles of Lost Creek

Michael's grandmother Jessie Ethel Hults was born on 10 June 1898 in Vigo County, on her father's farm in Lost Creek Township east of Terre Haute. The census of 1900 caught the household with the name spelled as the enumerator heard it, 'Gerris Hultz': Jennis Hubble Hults, 34, a farmer on his own mortgaged land, born in Vigo County in November 1865; his wife Dora, 35; Jessie, 1; her brother Leland, born that May; and two boys of 8 and 7, Floyd and Ernest, Jennis's sons by his first wife, Mattie Carrico. By 1910 the family had crossed the county line to Lewis Township in Clay County, and Jessie's marriage record of 1917 names her parents as James Hults and Dora Eversole, James being the clerk's best guess at a name nobody could spell. Her death certificate in 1991 has it 'Jennus.'

The Hults and Eversole lines are the oldest Vigo County lines on this page. Jennis's father, Joseph Bound Hults, was born in Butler County, Ohio, on 27 May 1830, the son of David Hults and Mary Bound, farmed in Clark County, Ohio, in 1860, and had settled in Riley Township, Vigo County, by 1870, where he died on 5 June 1904. Dora's father, Christopher Miller Eversole, born in Fairfield County, Ohio, on 9 July 1814 to Peter Eversole and Elizabeth Miller, married Nancy Ann Latta in Vigo County on 4 November 1841 and farmed at Lost Creek and Riley for forty years until his death on 6 June 1881; Eversole is the Ohio spelling of Ebersol, a name from the Pennsylvania German country. Emma Dora, born on 11 November 1864, was one of their youngest children. Her marriage to Jennis did not last: he married again in June 1922, and Dora died on 23 June 1928, at 63, and was buried at Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Terre Haute under a stone with two crosses and the line 'The cross leads generations on.' Jennis outlived her by nearly thirty years and died in Terre Haute on 12 February 1957, at 91.

Kentucky, Kansas and the Wabash, 1811 to 1950

Garrett and Sarah Smith: Bracken County Smiths and Larue County Killens

The Smith name comes down to Michael from Kentucky. Abraham Smith married Sarah McKinley in Bracken County, on the Ohio River upstream from Cincinnati, on 26 November 1811, and their son Robert McKinley Smith, born there on 29 June 1833, carried his mother's name as his middle name the way Michael carries his. Robert married Julia Ann Reagan, born 26 April 1831, a daughter of William Reagan and Sarah Adaline Collins, and raised a large family in Indiana: William Allen in 1852, Fannie in 1857, Samuel in 1858, Milton in 1863, Patsy in 1867, Garrett on 10 August 1873 and Thomas in 1875. The 1880 census has them in Wildcat Township, Tipton County, north of Indianapolis. Then the family went to Kansas, where Julia died in 1902 and Robert on 10 April 1914 in Montgomery County, and where Fannie, William and Thomas all died too; Garrett was the son who came back to Indiana. His Find a Grave memorial, indeed, gives his birthplace as Kansas, but the census takers of 1900, 1910 and 1930 all had it from him as Indiana.

Garrett R. Smith, 'Codge' to the people who knew him, married Sarah Elizabeth Killen in Vigo County on 21 August 1892, when he was nineteen and she seventeen. She had been born on 16 January 1875 in Larue County, Kentucky, Abraham Lincoln's birth county, the daughter of Christopher Columbus Killen, born in Kentucky in August 1853, and Nancy Ann DeSpain, born 12 August 1854 in Larue County to James Logan DeSpain and Sarah Ann Oaks, who had married on 5 March 1874. The Killens were at Otter Creek in Larue County in 1880 and in Indiana by the time Sarah married; her father, remarried, farmed in Posey Township, Clay County, in 1900, lived in Terre Haute in 1910 and died at Staunton, Clay County, on 14 September 1940, at 87. Sarah's brothers and sisters were Anna Margaret Timberman, Edward, John, Rebecca Modesitt and Semon.

Garrett and Sarah had six children on the rented farms of Honey Creek and Riley: Robert Wayne in April 1893, Pearl Ruby in November 1894, Mabel Marie in 1897, Hazel Irene in 1899, Esther Josephine in 1901 and Lida in 1904, who died as a girl. In 1900 Garrett was a farm laborer who had been out of work six months of the year. Sarah died on 15 October 1923, at 48, at Wabash Township in Clark County, Illinois, across the river from Terre Haute, and was brought home to Oak Hill Cemetery at Riley; the Tribune noticed her death on 16 October. Garrett lived on as a widower for twenty-seven years, a 'servant to the Boase family' in Honey Creek Township in 1930 in the census taker's phrase, a hired man in his fifties, and at Lost Creek in 1935 and 1940. He died in Terre Haute on 21 November 1950, at 77, when his great-grandson Michael was a year old, and was buried beside Sarah under a matching pink granite stone.

Santa Clara County, 1950s to 2012

Mark Avenue and the rocket plant

Sometime in the 1950s Ralph and Patricia Smith took their growing family west. The California directories pick them up in San Jose in 1964 and, from 1969, at 2961 Mark Avenue in Santa Clara, Ralph a technician; the same address and the same trade are in the 1974 directory, and it was the house Michael's brothers and sister grew up in. Ralph's employer was the United Technology Center at Sunnyvale, the rocket-motor division of United Aircraft that had opened in 1959 to build the big segmented solid-fuel boosters of the Titan III, the rockets that put the Air Force's satellites into orbit, with its test stands in the hills of the Coyote Valley south of San Jose. He retired from United Technologies in 1982, after the Sunnyvale plant had been his working life for the better part of twenty years. Ralph and Patricia's five children were Michael, Patricia Jean, Thomas, David and Ralph Wayne.

Patricia Bauer Smith died in Santa Clara on 12 July 2002, at 74, after fifty-four years of marriage. What Ralph did next is the coda to his 1945 wedding. Florence Jane Francis, whom he had married on a wartime furlough at eighteen and lost, had married Richard Fields in 1949 and been widowed in 1999; on 18 August 2005, in Vigo County, Ralph Warren Smith, 79, married Florence Jane Fields. She died at Carmel, Indiana, on 8 April 2006, seven months later, and his obituary would count her as his 'wife of seven months.' He went home to Terre Haute for good. Ralph W. Smith died at his home at Westminster Village, 1120 East Davis Drive, Terre Haute, on Tuesday, 7 February 2012, at 85. The Tribune-Star's obituary named his daughter Patricia Jean of San Jose; his sons Michael B. of San Mateo and wife Betty, Thomas E. of San Jose and wife Kristy, David A. of Livermore and wife Kathy, and Ralph Wayne of Alpharetta, Georgia, and wife Mary; his brother Paul and wife Yoshiko; and eleven grandchildren, among them 'Jason Goodwin and wife Petra of California, Robert Goodwin and wife Grace of Texas,' 'Dawn Goodwin of Pacifica' and 'Michelle Lewis and husband Tom of San Mateo.' After a visitation at DeBaun Springhill Chapel in Terre Haute on 11 February, his funeral was held in California on Friday, 17 February 2012, in St. Clare Chapel at Santa Clara Mission Cemetery, 490 Lincoln Street, and he was buried there. Patricia's grave is not recorded in any index online; the family will know whether it is beside his.

Santa Clara and San Mateo, 1950s to today

Michael, Betty and the five

Michael grew up in Santa Clara from the time he was a small boy, the eldest of Ralph and Patricia's five, and in the Vietnam years he went into the service and earned a paratrooper's wings; the family knows him as a Vietnam veteran, airborne. The unit, the years and the places are his to tell, and this page leaves room for them. He is a living man, and what is written here about his own life is what his family has said, not what the records say; the records of a life that is still being lived belong to him.

He married Elizabeth Anne Goodwin, Betty, the daughter of Robert Charles Goodwin and Peggy Lou Miller, born in San Mateo County on 29 May 1951, whose own family's story fills the companion pages of this site. The two names sit side by side in the printed record: in 1979 her mother's obituary named 'Betty Goodwin of San Mateo,' in 2005 her stepfather's named 'Betty Smith of San Mateo,' and in 2012 Ralph's named 'Michael B. Smith of San Mateo and wife Betty.' They made their home in San Mateo for more than thirty years. Betty has since died, and the date, like the date of their wedding, is for the family to add here. Their five children are Michael, Jason, Robert, Dawn and Michelle; Robert is Bobby, Grace's husband, for whom the family page on this site was made, and Bobby's daughter Elizabeth Lenora carries Betty's name.

Unfinished

What is still to be found

Michael's own birth notice has not been found, because his exact birthday is not yet on this page; the Terre Haute Tribune and Star printed the hospital births daily in 1949, and with the date the notice will be a ten-minute search. The 1948 wedding was surely written up in the Tribune's society pages, with the church, the attendants and the bride's dress, and that too is a search away. Anton Bauer's baptism is in the Stollhofen parish register on Matricula Online, Taufbuch 01/08, the 1881 to 1907 book, and a reader of the old German hand will find there his godparents, the house number at Frauendorf and his grandparents' names, one generation further back than this page reaches. The passenger list of his crossing in 1901 or 1902 has not been identified, and the Milwaukee naturalization of 1906 needs settling one way or the other. Patricia's obituary of July 2002 has not been located in the San Jose Mercury News, and the year the family moved from Terre Haute to California, which the birthplaces of Michael's brothers and sister would fix, is not yet known. Ralph's Army papers, his separation record and the 1st Cavalry Division's rosters would say where he was between Luzon and Tokyo; his Official Military Personnel File can be requested from the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis, and Pearl's, which would give his unit in France, likewise. Emma Alice Winters Beam's death has not been found, and Nancy Ann DeSpain's is given two ways by two sources. And Michael's Vietnam service, his marriage to Betty and her passing are the family's to add, and the page is built so that they can be.

Ahnentafel

  31. 1948Ralph marries Patricia Bauer on his twenty-second birthday, 28 May; registers for the peacetime draft as a Commercial Solvents watchman, 8 September
  32. 1949Michael Bauer Smith born in Terre Haute
  33. 1950Census, 1 April: Ralph, 23, laboratory technician, Patricia, 22, and Michael, 0, at 43 South 15th Street; Garrett Smith dies, 21 November
  34. 1950sThe family moves to California; San Jose by 1964
  35. 1957Jennis Hults dies in Terre Haute, 12 February
  36. 1969Ralph, technician, at 2961 Mark Avenue, Santa Clara, working for United Technology Center, Sunnyvale
  37. 1971Anton Bauer's 88th birthday noticed in the Tribune, 10 May
  38. 1973Ida Belle Bauer dies at home, 2800 Kussner Street, Terre Haute, 25 March; buried at Calvary
  39. 1977Anton Bauer dies in Terre Haute, 93, 2 March
  40. 1978Pearl Smith dies in Terre Haute, 83, 15 March; buried at Roselawn
  41. 1982Ralph retires from United Technologies, Sunnyvale
  42. 1991Jessie Hults Smith dies in Terre Haute, 93, 1 September
  43. 2002Patricia Bauer Smith dies in Santa Clara, 12 July, after 54 years of marriage
  44. 2005Ralph, 79, marries Florence Fields, his wife of 1945, in Vigo County, 18 August; she dies 8 April 2006
  45. 2012Ralph Warren Smith dies at Westminster Village, Terre Haute, 7 February; funeral at St. Clare Chapel, Santa Clara Mission Cemetery, 17 February
